## 4 Strategies to Avoid Common Token Inefficiencies

1. Use an appropriate model for each task.
2. Use memory files to indicate what is important for most tasks.
3. Start a new session if the current session has context that is not relevant to the task.
4. Convert input to machine-readable formats.

# Use Appropriate Models {background-color="#530153"}

## What Makes Different Models Different? How Do You Choose?

:::: {.columns .v-center-container}
::: {.column width="65%" }

* **Question:** If the biggest model is the most advanced model, why should I not always use it?

::: {.fragment}
* It is like asking: if my 18-wheel semi-truck is my most capable vehicle, why should I not use it to drive to the convenience store for a gallon of milk?

Using a semi-truck for this will work -- but if this is your habit, maxing out your household's fuel budget will not be mainly the fault of current gas prices.
:::

:::
::: {.column width="35%" }

::: {.fragment}
![](./img/truck-milk.jpg)
:::

:::
::::

## Models: What Differs and How to Choose?

- A bigger model can hold more detail, which would always be better if token cost and the environmental impact of data centers were not factors. However, that extra capacity is excessive for simple tasks.

::: {.fragment}
- While bigger models tend to be "_better_", they are not always the best choice when a task does not need that level of detail, because we would be paying for unused capacity.
:::
::: {.fragment}
- Example: a small model can be just as effective for proofreading a short paragraph. Using a larger model for this task is like taking a semi-truck to the convenience store.
:::
::: {.fragment}
- Choosing the right model is an art, not a science. Models constantly evolve, and smaller models today are more capable than large models were a year ago -- so it is impossible to give you a definitive list of tasks for each model.

A later slide in this presentation will show tools that can help you develop this skill by evaluating your model choice at the end of a task.
:::

# Use Memory Files {background-color="#530153"}

## Why Memory Files? My Agent Works Without Them

:::: {.columns .v-center-container}
::: {.column width="65%" }

* **Question:** Why do I need a memory file? My agent is really good at fetching all information in the project folder to find relevant information on its own.

::: {.fragment}
* It is like going to the grocery store and "_buying all items in the store just in case_", instead of using a shopping list and getting only what you need.

Buying "_all items in the grocery store_" each time you go there, and then throwing out what you did not use for dinner is wasteful and inefficient -- if you do that, it is not the current grocery prices' fault if you max out your household's grocery budget.

:::

:::
::: {.column width="35%" }

::: {.fragment}
![](./img/just-in-case-groceries.jpg)
:::

:::
::::

## My Agent Performs Well Without a Memory File

- Yes, your agent is likely to perform well without a memory file, but for each request, you will pay for rediscovering basic project-facts and while doing so consuming many tokens to parse through irrelevant information -- the AI companies will gladly take your money in return for doing this over and over again.

::: {.fragment}
- The memory file helps the agent find information efficiently. Don't make the agent waste tokens on extensive searches on each request when guidance for how to find it takes you a minute to write in the memory file. For example:
  - Where in the project folder is the code folder located?
  - Is data available in the project folder or what to do if it is not?
  - What programming languages are used for what tasks? (Scopes file formats to search for)
:::
::: {.fragment}
- With a memory file, the agent will, when needed, still search for and find additional context relevant to your request. But it does not start from nothing, will not buy all items in the grocery store when additional information is needed.
:::

# Start New Sessions {background-color="#530153"}

## Why Start New Sessions? It Is Easier to Keep Using the Same Chat

:::: {.columns .v-center-container}
::: {.column width="65%" }

* **Question:** Why can't I keep using the same chat for multiple tasks? It is faster and easier than constantly starting new chat sessions.

::: {.fragment}
* It is like going to the hardware store in an appropriate vehicle, but for each visit bring what you purchased in previous trips and pay for it again, and then add the new items in a new trailer to be paid for again and again. 

Even if you tell the agent to forget the previous part of the conversation, it will still have to process the full conversation regardless of whether that part is relevant or not.
:::

:::
::: {.column width="35%" }

::: {.fragment}
![](./img/line-of-trailers.jpg)
:::

:::
::::

## But it is Easier to Keep Using the Same Chat

- Models are stateless. This means that for each request, the full history of your session is sent to and processed by the language model -- including whatever the agent has added to the context window without your knowledge.
  - (_besides being cost-**_in_**efficient, long context windows risk diluting the model's attention with irrelevant information._)

::: {.fragment}
- This is repeated for each word generated by the model. **Yes. Each word!** (_Optimizations like caching exist, but fundamentally this is how it works, and caching still takes resources._)
:::
::: {.fragment}
- If you use the same chat session for, let's say, 10 tasks:
  - When the agent is generating a response for the second task, _you are paying again for the tokens used for the **first** task_. 
  - For the third task, _you are paying again for the **first** and **second** tasks_, and so on. 
  - For the tenth task, _you are paying for **all nine** previous tasks_ when generating the tenth response.
:::

# Use Machine Readable Inputs {background-color="#530153"}

## Why Do I Need to Convert Files? My AI agent can read Word and PDF files

:::: {.columns .v-center-container}
::: {.column width="65%" }

* **Question:** My team uses Word and PDF files, and my AI agent can read them. Why convert to plain text?

::: {.fragment}
* Asking a code assistant to re-convert a Word or PDF file for each prompt is like reprinting a book every time you want to look up a page.

Yes, your AI _can_ read all common formats, but agents that are not optimized for a particular file format will do so at a high token cost. Converting input files to machine-readable formats means you pay this cost only once.
:::

:::
::: {.column width="35%" }

::: {.fragment}
![](./img/reprint-books.jpg)
:::

:::
::::

## What are machine-readable formats?

Only plain text can be sent to a language model, so _plain-text_ formats can be sent as-is, but _binary files_ must be converted first.

Plain-text formats support the same text content with less formatting; binary formats support richer formatting but require computation to parse.

::: {.list-table}

- - File Type
  - _Plain Text Formats_
  - _Binary Formats_

- - Documents
  - `.txt`, `.md`, `.tex`, `.qmd`
  - `.doc`, `.docx`, `.pdf`

- - Presentations
  - `.tex` (beamer), `.qmd`
  - `.ppt`, `.pptx`, Google Slides

- - Spreadsheets
  - `.csv` (albeit limited)
  - `.xls`, `.xlsx`
  
:::

::: {.callout-note}

* While Microsoft Copilot is optimized for Microsoft formats like Word and Excel, it still needs to convert content to plain text before sending your data to the LLM -- but it is already optimized for this process.
* If your task only involves formatting or modifying Microsoft file formats, use Microsoft Copilot.
* The strategy on this slide is most relevant when you use Claude Code or GitHub Copilot for code tasks where binary formats are repeatedly used as inputs -- Microsoft Copilot is not optimized for writing code and does not do so well.

:::


## 3 strategies for machine-readable formats

::: {.list-table}

- - Category
  - _Convert with AI_
  - _Write a script with AI_
  - _Plain text first_

- - Description
  - Prompt the AI to convert the file and save it in a plain-text format, then tell AI to use that file.
  - Prompt the AI to write a reusable script to convert the file.
  - Use plain text in the first place, and only convert to binary for dissemination to humans.

- - Use Cases
  - You have a single document that is never updated to convert 
  - You have many similar documents to convert, or a single document that changes often
  - Your project is to produce these files, and you use AI to generate or review them

- - Review Need
  - You need to review the conversion ad hoc for this one file.
  - You need to test the script on several files before trusting it generally.
  - No conversion is needed -- many plain-text formats can be reliably converted to binary formats.

:::

## Advice for conversion scripts

- If the relevant content of your files consists only of text or data, the AI should have no problem writing a script that converts the files reliably.
- If formatting carries information, font color has meaning, or diagrams and images are used, you are likely to have to spend more time on that script.

::: {.fragment}
- For spreadsheets, there are very reliable libraries to convert between CSV and Excel formats. For example, Python's `pandas` can convert data between Excel formats and `.csv` in both directions. However, CSV has no support for formatting such as merged cells, so that information is lost.
- For Word and PDF files, libraries exist to extract text. Text is reliably converted, but information from images, diagrams, tables, page references, and so on might be lost or incorrectly converted.
:::

::: {.fragment}
- AI will change how we work, perhaps even what our default file formats are:
  - Personal computers made us use Excel and Word instead of pen and paper or typewriters.
  - The internet made us use email instead of sending letters. 
  - Will AI make us use machine-readable formats for work-in-progress and use Word/Excel/PDF only for human dissemination?
:::
